hints: Think about which of the three can most easily release $\text{H}^{+}$. Which one is not even an acid but a neutral amide?
Compare $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. What property of chlorine affects electron density in the molecule?
Link electron withdrawal to the $\text{O-H}$ bond strength and to the stability of the carboxylate anion left after $\text{H}^{+}$ is lost.
walkthrough:
Sort out who is an acid at all**
Picture what acidity means: how easily a molecule gives away $\text{H}^{+}$ from its $\text{O-H}$ group. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONH}_{2}$ has no acidic $\text{O-H}$, only $\text{N-H}$ bonds that do not ionise in water. It is essentially neutral, so it must sit at the least acidic end.

Compare the two real carboxylic acids**
Both $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ can lose $\text{H}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$ and $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$. The only difference is three $\text{Cl}$ atoms replacing three $\text{H}$ atoms on the adjacent carbon. Chlorine is very electronegative, so it pulls electron density toward itself through sigma bonds.

Link withdrawal to easier proton loss**
That electron withdrawing inductive effect pulls charge away from the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ group. It weakens and polarises the $\text{O-H}$ bond, making $\text{H}^{+}$ easier to release. Just as important, the negative charge on the $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$ anion is spread and stabilised, so the equilibrium $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{A}^{-}$ lies further to the right. Hence $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ is the strongest acid.

Final answer: ethanamide < ethanoic acid < trichloroethanoic acid (least to most acidic).
Ethanamide is neutral and is not a proton donor.
Chlorine atoms are electronegative and electron withdrawing by the inductive effect, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond and stabilising the anion, so trichloroethanoic acid donates $\text{H}^{+}$ most readily.

hints: Recall what functional group Fehling's reagent oxidises, and look for that hidden group inside $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the hidden aldehyde**
Fehling's reagent oxidises aldehydes but not ketones or ordinary acids. Draw $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$ as $\text{H-C(=O)-OH}$. It contains an $\text{H-C=O}$ unit just like an aldehyde, so it can be oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$ and water while reducing blue $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to red $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$. Ethanoic acid and ethanedioic acid lack this easily oxidised $\text{H-C=O}$ group under these mild conditions.
Final answer: methanoic acid only.

hints: Warm acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ is a much stronger oxidant than Fehling's, so think which acids can still be oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Use a stronger oxidant**
Warm acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ will oxidise any strong reducing acid to $\text{CO}_{2}$, decolourising purple $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ to colourless $\text{Mn}^{2+}$. Methanoic acid $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$ is oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$, and ethanedioic acid $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCO}_{2}\text{H}$ is also readily oxidised to $2\text{CO}_{2}$. Ethanoic acid $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ has no oxidisable $\text{C-H}$ or $\text{C-C}$ linkage of this type and does not react.
Final answer: methanoic acid and ethanedioic acid.

hints: Ethanoic acid must be converted into a much more reactive carbonyl compound containing Cl before ammonia can form the amide.
Replace the $\text{-OH}$ of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ by $\text{-Cl}$ and name the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ group as ethanoyl.
walkthrough:
Build the reactive intermediate**
Carboxylic acids react too slowly with ammonia to give amides directly on heating in good yield. The standard route is to first make the acyl chloride. Swapping $\text{-OH}$ for $\text{-Cl}$ gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-C(=O)-Cl}$, written $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$.

Name it correctly**
The $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ fragment is the ethanoyl group, so $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ is ethanoyl chloride.

Final answer: structural formula: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$
name: ethanoyl chloride.

hints: Recall the three standard reagents that replace $\text{-OH}$ by $\text{-Cl}$ in a carboxylic acid.
Think what nucleophile attacks the acyl chloride to replace $\text{-Cl}$ by $\text{-NH}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Make the acyl chloride**
Use phosphorus(V) chloride $\text{PCl}_{5}$, phosphorus(III) chloride $\text{PCl}_{3}$, or thionyl chloride $\text{SOCl}_{2}$. For example: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} + \text{SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$$ All three do the same job of substituting $\text{Cl}$ for $\text{OH}$.

Convert to the amide**
Add ammonia $\text{NH}_{3}$, often in excess and at room temperature: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} + 2\text{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CONH}_{2} + \text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$$ Ammonia acts as nucleophile then as base to remove $\text{HCl}$.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{PCl}_{5}$ or $\text{PCl}_{3}$ or $\text{SOCl}_{2}$
step 2: $\text{NH}_{3}$ (ammonia).

hints: Remember proton NMR only detects $^{1}\text{H}$, so consider whether the solvent itself contains $^{1}\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Keep the solvent invisible**
Proton NMR detects $^{1}\text{H}$ nuclei. Ordinary $\text{CHCl}_{3}$ has one proton and would produce a huge absorption that swamps the sample peaks. Replacing $\text{H}$ by deuterium $\text{D}$ ($^{2}\text{H}$) gives $\text{CDCl}_{3}$, which has no $^{1}\text{H}$ to resonate, so only the amide protons are seen.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_{3}$ contains no $^{1}\text{H}$ so gives no signal, whereas $\text{CHCl}_{3}$ contains $^{1}\text{H}$ and would give a large solvent peak.

hints: Match peak areas to proton counts: the tall singlet near $\delta$ 2 is the 3H $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C=O}$, the quartet near $\delta$ 1.2 is the 3H ethyl $\text{CH}_{3}$.
The $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to N is deshielded to about $\delta$ 3.3, while the $\text{N-H}$ proton appears well downfield near $\delta$ 6.8.
walkthrough:
Assign the two methyl groups**
Look at integration and splitting. The sharp singlet at $\delta$ about 2.0 with area 3H is the $\text{CH}_{3}$ attached directly to $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONH-}$, no neighbours to split it. The triplet-like multiplet at $\delta$ about 1.2 with area 3H is the ethyl $\text{CH}_{3}$ in $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, split by the adjacent $\text{CH}_{2}$.

Assign the deshielded protons**
The multiplet near $\delta$ 3.3 is the $\text{N-CH}_{2}$ group, pulled downfield by electronegative N and the carbonyl. The broad singlet near $\delta$ 6.8 with area 1H is the amide $\text{N-H}$, strongly deshielded by the carbonyl and N and showing no clear splitting.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C=O}$: $\delta$ 1.9 to 2.1; $\text{N-H}$: $\delta$ 6.5 to 7.0; $\text{N-CH}_{2}$: $\delta$ 3.0 to 3.5; $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$: $\delta$ 1.0 to 1.5.

hints: Identify which proton in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONHC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ is acidic enough to exchange with a protic solvent.
Recall what happens to an exchangeable $^{1}\text{H}$ signal when $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ is added and why D is invisible in proton NMR.
walkthrough:
Spot the labile proton**
Amide $\text{N-H}$ protons are labile and exchange rapidly with protic solvents. In $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ the equilibrium $\text{N-H} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{N-D} + \text{HOD}$ occurs.

Explain the missing peak**
Deuterium resonates at a completely different frequency and is not detected in a $^{1}\text{H}$ spectrum. So the $\text{N-H}$ absorption near $\delta$ 6.8 vanishes, while the $\text{C-H}$ peaks for the methyl and methylene groups remain unchanged because $\text{C-H}$ protons do not exchange.

Final answer: The peak at $\delta$ 6.6 to 6.8 due to $\text{N-H}$ disappears.
The $\text{N-H}$ proton exchanges with D from $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ to give $\text{N-D}$, which gives no proton signal.

hints: Calculate the $M_{r}$ of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONHC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ and think which bond cleavage leaves a fragment of mass 58 containing C, H, N and O.
walkthrough:
Work out the fragment**
$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONHC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ has $M_{r} = 87$. A peak at $m/e = 58$ corresponds to loss of an ethyl fragment ($29$). Cleavage of the $\text{N-C}$ ethyl bond leaves $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-C(=O)-NH}^{+}$. Adding masses: $2(12) + 4(1) + 14 + 16 = 58$, so the ion is $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{4}\text{NO}^{+}$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{4}\text{NO}^{+}$ ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONH}^{+}$).

hints: Converting $\text{C=O}$ in an amide to $\text{CH}_{2}$ to give an amine needs a very powerful hydride reducing agent.
walkthrough:
Choose the strong reducer**
The change $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONHC}_{2}\text{H}_{5} \rightarrow \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{NHC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ is reduction of the carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}$. Amides need the strong reducing agent lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$, in dry ether followed by aqueous work up. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is too weak for this.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ (lithium aluminium hydride).

hints: Draw $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{NHC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ and check whether the two ethyl groups are in identical environments.
walkthrough:
Count carbon environments**
Diethylamine is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. The molecule is symmetric, the two $\text{CH}_{3}$ carbons are equivalent to each other and the two $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons are equivalent to each other. That gives just two distinct $^{13}\text{C}$ absorptions, one for $\text{CH}_{3}$ and one for $\text{CH}_{2}$.
Final answer: 2.
